description: We are a team of two computer science students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We aim to combine creativity, research, and web development to create interactive solutions that make space exploration more accessible and engaging. Through our project, Space Graveyard, we document the legacy of human-made machines left behind on the Moon and Mars, highlighting their missions, scientific contributions, and lasting impact on space exploration.
summary:
Space Graveyard is an interactive, dark-sky astronomical web museum built to commemorate these inactive exploratory craft.
Designed with an aesthetic inspired by NASA mission dashboards and high-contrast observatory interfaces, the platform offers an educational journey:
Curated Mission Dossiers: Deep dives into iconic abandoned artifacts on the Moon (Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, Apollo Lunar Module Descent Stages, Luna 2) and Mars (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix).
Interactive Filtering & Destinational Exploration: Dual-mode lunar and Martian habitat views with regional landing coordinates and environmental overviews.
Chronological Mission Timeline: A unified historical narrative charting robotic space exploration from the earliest 1959 impact to modern deep-space robotic veterans.
Interactive Detailed Telemetry Modals: Comprehensive readouts highlighting mission objectives, scientific yields, terminal conditions, and contemporary relevance with direct links to official NASA records.
Scientific Legacy Analysis: An analytical exploration of the engineering lessons, technological spin-offs, and heritage-site policies stemming from these abandoned machines.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?
Space Graveyard is an interactive web museum for seven NASA robotic missions left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors browse mission cards, filter by Moon or Mars, and open a dossier for each machine covering its purpose, achievements, what ended the mission and its last location. They can also explore a timeline and a legacy section. It runs in the browser from one data file, with no backend.

Benefits
It makes verified NASA mission history easy and engaging for anyone to explore. It is free, works on phones and desktops, and needs no installation.

Intended impact
To show that inactive machines are scientific milestones and heritage sites, not “space junk”. It also keeps their lessons visible for Artemis and future Mars missions.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Fonts: Orbitron and Inter, from Google Fonts.
  • Tools: VS Code with Live Server, and Git and GitHub.
  • Data and images: NASA Science, NASA NSSDC, the NASA Image and Video Library and the JPL Photojournal.
  • Hardware: an ordinary laptop. If you used any AI tools, add them here, since many hackathons ask for that to be disclosed.

How is it creative?
It treats abandoned spacecraft as a museum, using an observatory-style dark interface with an animated starfield and counters that count up as you scroll. Each machine is presented as a story, from launch to its final silence.

What factors did the team consider?
We considered factual accuracy (every fact is cross-checked against NASA sources), accessibility (keyboard navigation and ARIA labels), and responsive design from phones to wide screens. We also kept it simple to run, with no build step, so anyone can open it instantly.
